claim: During odor plume navigation, walking Drosophila melanogaster bias their motion upwind in response to the frequency of their encounters with the odor.
source: We and others have shown that during odor plume navigation, walking Drosophila melanogaster bias their motion upwind in response to both the frequency of their encounters with the odor (Demir et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Demir et al., 2020, which is prior experimental work.

claim: During odor plume navigation, walking Drosophila melanogaster bias their motion upwind in response to the intermittency of the odor signal.
source: We and others have shown that during odor plume navigation, walking Drosophila melanogaster bias their motion upwind in response to both the frequency of their encounters with the odor (Demir et al., 2020) and the intermittency of the odor signal, which we define to be the fraction of time the signal is above a detection threshold (Alvarez-Salvado et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alvarez-Salvado et al., 2018, which is prior experimental work.

claim: Navigators that only use frequency or intermittency perform well in some environments but fail in others.
source: Through agent-based simulations, we find that navigators that only use frequency or intermittency perform well in some environments – achieving maximal performance when gains are near those inferred from experiment – but fail in others.
evidence: The claim is supported by agent-based simulations performed in this study, as described in the abstract and detailed in the Results section.

claim: Robust performance across diverse environments requires both temporal modalities (frequency and intermittency).
source: Robust performance across diverse environments requires both temporal modalities.
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3-5.

claim: There is a steep trade-off when using both sensors simultaneously.
source: However, we also find a steep trade-off when using both sensors simultaneously, suggesting a strong benefit to modulating how much each sensor is weighted, rather than using both in a fixed combination across plumes.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results, particularly shown in Figure 4I which demonstrates the Pareto front.

claim: The circuitry of the Drosophila olfactory periphery naturally enables simultaneous intermittency and frequency sensing.
source: Finally, we show that the circuitry of the Drosophila olfactory periphery naturally enables simultaneous intermittency and frequency sensing, enhancing robust navigation through a diversity of odor environments.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling of ORN and PN circuits based on prior work (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Nagel et al., 2015) and simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The first stage of olfactory processing selects and encodes temporal features of odor signals critical to real-world navigation tasks.
source: Together, our results suggest that the first stage of olfactory processing selects and encodes temporal features of odor signals critical to real-world navigation tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and simulation results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Turbulent flows produce rapid changes in local odor concentrations.
source: Turbulent flows produce rapid changes in the local odor concentrations, and instantaneous odor gradients often do not point toward the source (Celani et al., 2014; Crimaldi and Koseff, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on turbulent odor plumes.

claim: Instantaneous odor gradients often do not point toward the source in turbulent flows.
source: Turbulent flows produce rapid changes in the local odor concentrations, and instantaneous odor gradients often do not point toward the source (Celani et al., 2014; Crimaldi and Koseff, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Encounters between the animal and odorized packets of air are intermittent, with durations and frequencies spanning many orders of magnitude.
source: Encounters between the animal and odorized packets of air are intermittent, with durations and frequencies spanning many orders of magnitude (Celani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Near boundaries and with lower mean wind speeds, odor plumes are smoother, with odor concentrations consistently above detectable thresholds.
source: Moreover, distinct flow conditions result in distinct spatiotemporal statistics: near boundaries and with lower mean wind speeds, odor plumes are smoother, with odor concentrations consistently above detectable thresholds (Connor et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Roughness in the physical landscape and shifting winds can cause plumes to break up into discrete odor filaments, interspersed with long periods of undetectable concentrations.
source: But roughness in the physical landscape – sands, rough terrain, vegetation – and shifting winds can cause plumes to break up into discrete odor filaments, interspersed with long periods of undetectable concentrations (Cardé and Willis, 2008; Murlis et al., 1992; Riffell et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Encounters with odor filaments can occur over a wide range of frequencies from 0.1 Hz to 5 Hz or more.
source: There, encounters with odor filaments can occur over a wide range of frequencies from 0.1 Hz (Riffell et al., 2008) to 5 Hz or more (Demir et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Many organisms have evolved olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) that respond to chemical signals with high temporal precision.
source: Indeed, many organisms have evolved olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) that respond to chemical signals with high temporal precision (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Jacob et al., 2017; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Szyszka et al., 2014; Szyszka et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: ORN firing responses are strongly time-locked to the arrival time of an odor.
source: ORN firing responses are strongly time-locked to the arrival time of an odor (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Fast synaptic mechanisms allow ORN information to be passed quickly downstream to projection neurons within milliseconds.
source: and fast synaptic mechanisms (Fox and Nagel, 2021; Martelli et al., 2013) allow this information to be passed quickly downstream, within milliseconds, to projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe, driving rapid behavioral responses (Bhandawat et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Drosophila ORNs adapt their firing rates and gain to prolonged stimuli.
source: In addition to these fast responses, Drosophila ORNs also adapt their firing rates and gain to prolonged stimuli (Cao et al., 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Nagel and Wilson, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ORN adaptation primes ORNs to accurately encode future odor signals without losing temporal precision as intensity changes.
source: priming them to accurately encode future odor signals (Kadakia and Emonet, 2019) without losing temporal precision as intensity changes (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Martelli et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In honeybees, the temporal resolution of odor pulses increases over time in a pulsed odor environment.
source: Likewise, in honeybees, the temporal resolution of odor pulses increases over time in a pulsed odor environment (Szyszka et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the moth Agrotis ipsilon, ORN responses adjust to optimally encode odor signals that occur most frequently in the environment.
source: while in the moth Agrotis ipsilon, ORN responses adjust to optimally encode odor signals that occur most frequently in the environment (Levakova et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Olfactory neurons in insects are sensitive to the temporal features of odor signals on both short and long timescales.
source: Olfactory neurons in insects are thus sensitive to the temporal features of odor signals on both short and long timescales (Nagel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work and is a summary statement based on the preceding evidence.

claim: In mice, plume dynamics as fast as tens of milliseconds are encoded downstream in mitral and tufted cells.
source: In mice, plume dynamics as fast as tens of milliseconds are encoded downstream in mitral and tufted cells (Ackels et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In crustaceans, odors are encoded by bursting ORNs which burst only if odors arrive at some phase relative to an intrinsic bursting cycle.
source: In crustaceans, odors are encoded by bursting ORNs (or bORNs), which burst only if odors arrive at some phase relative to an intrinsic bursting cycle (Park et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Bursting cycles in crustacean ORNs vary over orders of magnitudes across the bORN population, providing a natural template to encode the timing between odor arrivals.
source: These cycles vary over orders of magnitudes across the bORN population, providing a natural template to encode the timing between odor arrivals (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Flying male moths fly faster and straighter upwind when receiving odor hits at higher frequencies than lower ones.
source: When tracking pheromones, flying male moths fly faster and straighter upwind when receiving odor hits at higher frequencies than lower ones (Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994; Vickers and Baker, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Walking silkworm moths switch from zigzagging motion to straighter trajectories upwind in higher-frequency environments.
source: Walking silkworm moths switch from zigzagging motion to straighter trajectories upwind in higher-frequency environments (Kanzaki et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: One model has suggested that odor hits suppress an otherwise persistent internal counterturning mechanism in moths.
source: One model (Vickers and Baker, 1994) has suggested that odor hits suppress an otherwise persistent internal counterturning mechanism, allowing moths to maintain straight trajectories if odors are frequent or long.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior modeling work.

claim: Flying flies counterturn shortly after passing through the odor, indicating that counterturning can be driven by the loss of the plume.
source: Alternatively, flying flies counterturn shortly after passing through the odor (Budick and Dickinson, 2006; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014), indicating that counterturning can be also driven by the loss of the plume rather than an internal mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Crabs navigate successfully in environments with higher-odor intermittency, but fail to find odor sources as pulses become more infrequent.
source: In water, crabs navigate successfully in environments with higher-odor intermittency, but fail to find odor sources as pulses become more infrequent (Keller and Weissburg, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Walking flies maintained upwind headings and increased walking speed over the duration of odor pulses in spatially uniform but temporally varying environments.
source: One of these (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018) focused on spatially uniform but temporally varying environments, where the odor was presented in spatially uniform pulses lasting anywhere from 1 to 10 s. In this environment, walking flies maintained upwind headings and increased walking speed over the duration of the odor pulses, albeit with a degree of desensitization over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: In spatiotemporally complex odor plumes, fly navigation was reproduced by a model in which only the frequency of odor encounters controlled upwind orientation, independent of their duration or concentration.
source: The second study (Demir et al., 2020) instead challenged flies to navigate spatiotemporally complex odor plumes that were generated by stochastically perturbing a thin ribbon of odor. In this plume, odor encounters were much shorter (~0.1–0.3 s), more frequent (~3 Hz), and less predictable. In that study, fly navigation was reproduced by a model in which only the frequency of odor encounters controlled upwind orientation, independent of their duration or concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The dynamical model proposed by Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018 picks out odor signal intermittency in appropriate limits.
source: We first demonstrate analytically that the dynamical model proposed in the first study above picks out (in appropriate limits) odor signal intermittency, while the model in the second study responds to the frequency of odor hits.
evidence: The claim is supported by analytical derivations presented in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The model from Demir et al., 2020 responds to the frequency of odor hits.
source: We first demonstrate analytically that the dynamical model proposed in the first study above picks out (in appropriate limits) odor signal intermittency, while the model in the second study responds to the frequency of odor hits.
evidence: The claim is supported by analytical derivations presented in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The combined model requires both sensors to successfully navigate both measured plumes used in the two studies.
source: Using agent-based simulations, we first show that this combined model requires both sensors to successfully navigate both measured plumes used in the two studies.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: To robustly navigate a variety of plumes agents should use both intermittency and frequency sensing.
source: We find that to robustly navigate a variety of plumes agents should use both intermittency and frequency sensing.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: There is a trade-off in performance when using both temporal features simultaneously, which persists across a variety of plumes.
source: However, there is a trade-off in performance when using both temporal features simultaneously, which persists across a variety of plumes.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: PNs respond independently to both frequency and intermittency features and enable effective navigation through various environments.
source: We find that PNs respond independently to both features and enable effective navigation through various environments, suggesting that the first stage of olfactory processing is appropriately tuned for naturalistic navigation tasks.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The adaptive Hill function mimics the gain adaptation of ORNs to the mean signal.
source: This mimics the gain adaptation of ORNs to the mean signal (Cao et al., 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on ORN adaptation.

claim: Both the intermittency and frequency models are sensitive to the temporal characteristics of the signal, but not absolute concentration.
source: Note that both models are sensitive to the temporal characteristics of the signal, but not absolute concentration.
evidence: This is a property of the mathematical models as described.

claim: The intermittency model was first extracted from flies navigating a uniformly odorized region of odor within a laminar airflow.
source: The intermittency model was first extracted from flies navigating a uniformly odorized region of odor within a laminar airflow (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The intermittency model qualitatively recapitulates navigational behavior in a measured near-bed turbulent plume.
source: Using simulations, the model was then shown to qualitatively recapitulate navigational behavior in a measured near-bed turbulent plume (Connor et al., 2018; Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: In the high-intermittency plume, the odor signal was ever-present and varied on relatively long timescales of several seconds or more.
source: which we call the high-intermittency plume, in which the odor signal was ever-present and varied on relatively long timescales of several seconds or more (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B showing the plume characteristics.

claim: The frequency model was fit to trajectories of flies navigating a plume with a high degree of spatial complexity generated by perturbing a fast laminar flow with stochastic lateral jets.
source: In contrast, the frequency model was fit to trajectories of flies navigating a plume with a high degree of spatial complexity (Figure 2D) generated by perturbing a fast laminar flow with stochastic lateral jets, which we call the high-frequency plume.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup from prior work (Demir et al., 2020).

claim: In the high-frequency plume, odor whiffs occurred frequently (2–5 Hz) and were much shorter (~100 ms).
source: In that experiment, odor whiffs occurred frequently (2–5 Hz) (Figure 2E and F) and were much shorter (~100 ms) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 2E and 2F showing the plume characteristics.

claim: In the high-intermittency plume, odor intermittency reached as high as 100% and whiff frequencies rarely surpassed 1 Hz.
source: in the first, odor intermittency reached as high as 100% and whiff frequencies rarely surpassed 1 Hz (Figure 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2C showing the plume statistics.

claim: In the high-frequency plume, the signal had intermittency mostly below 30% but whiff frequencies of several Hz.
source: whereas in the latter, the signal had intermittency mostly below 30% but whiff frequencies of several Hz (Figure 2F).

claim: Odor signals influence many behavioral actions, including accelerating, turning, and stopping.
source: It is known that odor signals influence many behavioral actions, including accelerating, turning, and stopping (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Baker and Vickers, 1997; Demir et al., 2020; Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994; Vickers and Baker, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Insects nearly universally turn upwind or bias their turns upwind in the presence of odor.
source: Given the near-universal response of insects to turn upwind or bias their turns upwind in the presence of odor (Baker et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Individual trajectories of successful flies in either plume show that agents quickly reorient within the plume region and navigate to the source with relatively straight trajectories combined with occasional corrective kinks.
source: Individual trajectories of successful flies in either plume look similar: when oriented away from the source, agents are quickly able to reorient within the plume region and navigate to the source with relatively straight trajectories combined with occasional corrective kinks (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Agents navigated successfully in both the high-intermittency and high-frequency plumes using the combined model.
source: Overall, agents navigated successfully in both plumes (Figure 3C), and performance was relatively robust to initial angle and position (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: A simple linear combination of intermittency and frequency sensors robustly navigates two disparate odor plumes without obvious failure modes due to interference between sensors.
source: This suggests that a simple linear combination robustly navigates two disparate odor plumes, without exhibiting any obvious failure modes due to interference between sensors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The intermittency sensor dominates in the high-intermittency plume, whereas the frequency sensor dominates in the high-frequency plume.
source: As expected, the intermittency sensor dominates in the high-intermittency plume, whereas the frequency sensor dominates in the high-frequency plume (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Frequency sensing plays a role near the conical boundary of the high-intermittency plume.
source: For example, frequency sensing plays a role near the conical boundary of the high-intermittency plume.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Intermittency contributes along the centerline of the high-frequency plume.
source: Likewise, intermittency contributes along the centerline of the high-frequency plume.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the simulated high-frequency plume, a variety of gains led to similarly maximal performance, including some with values an order of magnitude larger than the base gains.
source: However, in the simulated high-frequency plume, a variety of gains led to similarly maximal performance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), including some with values an order of magnitude larger than the base gains.

claim: Adding Gaussian noise to the I and F filters removed maxima at high gains but retained clear maxima at lower gains.
source: We therefore added Gaussian noise to the I and F filters – noise amplitude was 5% of the average value of I (F) in the center of the simulated high-intermittency (high-frequency) plume. This removed maxima at high gains but retained clear maxima at lower gains (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: The unique maxima in performance sat fairly close to the base gain values, suggesting a degree of tuning within the biological fly olfactory circuit.
source: Interestingly, the unique maxima sat fairly close to the base gain values (values of 1 in Figure 4G and H), suggesting a degree of tuning within the biological fly olfactory circuit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: Optimal performance in either plume requires silencing the nonrelevant sensors.
source: indicating that optimal performance in either plume requires silencing the nonrelevant sensors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The inherent trade-off illustrates that simply augmenting the sensory capability can at times degrade performance.
source: This inherent trade-off illustrates that simply augmenting the sensory capability can at times degrade performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: There was no fixed set of gains that performs optimally in both plumes.
source: There was no fixed set of gains that performs optimally in both plumes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The apparent concavity of the Pareto front illustrates a somewhat steep trade-off and suggests that flies might be better off modulating gains and switching between using intermittency and frequency sensors.
source: Importantly, the apparent concavity of the Pareto front illustrates a somewhat steep trade-off and suggests that flies might be better off modulating gains and switching between using intermittency and frequency sensors to bias upwind motion, as opposed to using both simultaneously.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 4I.

claim: A trade-off in navigational performance persists across a wide range of odor environments.
source: exemplifying a trade-off in navigational performance that persists across this wide range of odor environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: While a naïve summation of temporal sensors may be beneficial in some cases, in general, navigation can always be improved by some degree of specialization.
source: Together with the results presented above (Figure 3), this suggests that while a naïve summation of temporal sensors may be beneficial in some cases, in general, navigation can always be improved by some degree of specialization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Prior experimental and modeling work has shown that synaptic and circuit mechanisms in the olfactory periphery allow for accurate signal transmission across a range of frequencies.
source: Prior experimental and modeling work has shown that synaptic and circuit mechanisms in the olfactory periphery allow for accurate signal transmission across a range of frequencies (Martelli and Fiala, 2019; Nagel et al., 2015)

claim: Fast ORN adaptation allows signals to be encoded without saturation.

source: These various mechanisms suggest that the natural structure of the fly olfactory circuit may be well-primed for robust encoding of multiple temporal features of the odor signal.

claim: Average PN membrane potential increases with frequency and intermittency independently.
source: We find that average membrane potential increases with frequency and intermittency independently (Figure 6B).

claim: The circuit-inspired model was outperformed by the single-sensor models when these were used in matching environments.

claim: The manner in which temporal features are extracted and processed within the Drosophila olfactory circuit may already be adapted to natural plume environments.
source: This suggests that the manner in which temporal features are extracted and processed within the Drosophila olfactory circuit may already be adapted to natural plume environments.

claim: More diverse actions such as stopping and walking, speed modulation, continuous heading modulation, and casting/counter-turning behavior have been observed in insect olfactory navigation.
source: However, more diverse actions such as stopping and walking (Demir et al., 2020), speed modulation (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994), continuous heading modulation (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018), and casting/counter-turning behavior Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Budick and Dickinson, 2006; Mafra-Neto and Cardé, 1994; Pang et al., 2018; Vickers and Baker, 1994 have also been observed in insect olfactory navigation.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Infotaxis, where agents navigate by using cues to learn an internal probabilistic representation of their environment, has some support in experiment.
source: Theoretical strategies such as infotaxis, where agents navigate by using cues to learn an internal probabilistic representation of their environment (Vergassola et al., 2007), also have some support in experiment (Calhoun et al., 2014; Pang et al., 2018).
